## The big idea

Whatever momentum flux crosses your control surface, something must push
back: $\sum \mathbf{F} = \dot m\, \Delta \mathbf{V}$ for steady flow.
This is how fluids exert forces on the world — jets, bends, nozzles,
rockets — and, in one of the great arguments of the unit, how much power
the wind will ever surrender to a turbine: **16/27 of what's passing
through, and not a joule more.**

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: C_P (and its ceiling, 16/27)
The power coefficient — extracted power over the wind power through the
rotor disk. Betz proved its maximum is 16/27 ≈ 0.593 using nothing but
this module's tools. Modern turbines reach ~0.45–0.50: engineering has
nearly caught the theorem.
:::

## The ledger, now with direction

The momentum version of the transport theorem, steady flow:

$$\sum \mathbf{F} = \oint_{CS} \rho\, \mathbf{u}\,(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{n})\, dS$$

— for uniform openings, $\sum \mathbf{F} = \sum \dot m\, \mathbf{V}_\text{out} -
\sum \dot m\, \mathbf{V}_\text{in}$. Left side: *every* force on the CV's
contents — pressure on the openings (gauge pressure, if the CV is bathed
in atmosphere: the atmosphere's push cancels around any closed surface),
gravity, and the reaction from any solid the CV touches or cuts. That
last one is usually the unknown you're after, which is why cutting the CV
*through the bolts* is the signature move: slice through the flange
bolts of a pipe bend and the bolt tension appears, exposed, on the left
side of a vector equation you can solve.

The discipline that makes it work is the same ceremony as 5.1, now with
consequences squared: momentum is a **vector** ledger, one equation per
direction, with $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{n}$ setting flux signs and the
velocity itself carrying its own sign separately. (The porous pipe's part
(e): the outflow leaves *radially* — carrying zero axial momentum — while
axial momentum enters at the inlet. Something must absorb the difference:
the pipe is pushed **downstream**, and the same integral as 5.1 with one
more factor of velocity prices it. Intuition and ledger agree, which is
the point of having both.)

The toolbox handles the standard cases — `jet_on_flat_plate`,
`jet_on_curved_vane`, `bend_anchor_force`, `nozzle_thrust` — and the
verify-then-apply homework has you beat one of them by hand first. Be
wary of the classic traps: forgetting the *pressure* forces on the
openings of a pressurized bend (momentum flux is often the *smaller*
load!), and reporting the force on the fluid when the question asked for
the force on the anchor (Newton's third law: same number, opposite sign,
different sentence).

## Betz: how much will the wind give up?

Now the unit's crown jewel, because it uses mass, momentum, *and* energy
in one argument. A wind turbine, idealized as a disk of area $A$, sits in
wind $U_1$. Downstream, the air has slowed to $U_2$ — it *must* still be
moving; the air has to leave. Draw the stream tube through the disk.
Mass: fixed $\dot m$ through the tube. Momentum: thrust on the disk $T =
\dot m (U_1 - U_2)$. Energy: power extracted $P = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot m
(U_1^2 - U_2^2)$. Combine them (one clean step: the velocity *at the
disk* comes out as the average of far-up and far-downstream) and
normalize by the wind power through $A$:

$$C_P = \frac{P}{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho A U_1^3}
= \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - r^2\right)\left(1 + r\right), \qquad r = U_2/U_1.$$

The trade is now visible: slow the wind a *lot* (small $r$) and each kilo
surrenders lots of energy — but slow air clogs the tube and $\dot m$
starves. Slow it a *little* and mass streams through — carrying its
energy away with it. Somewhere between is the sweet spot:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof r_53 = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.98], {value: 0.6, step: 0.01, label: "r = U₂/U₁ (how much you slow the wind)"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - r_53
r = np.linspace(0.001, 1, 300)
Cp = 0.5*(1-r**2)*(1+r)
Cp_pt = 0.5*(1-r_53**2)*(1+r_53)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4))
ax.plot(r, Cp, lw=2.5)
ax.plot(r_53, Cp_pt, 'o', ms=11, mfc='gold', mec='k')
ax.axhline(16/27, color='crimson', ls='--', lw=1.5)
ax.annotate(' Betz limit 16/27 ≈ 0.593  (at r = 1/3)', (0.02, 16/27+0.012),
            color='crimson', fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlabel('r = U₂/U₁'); ax.set_ylabel('C_P')
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.68); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title(f"your setting: C_P = {Cp_pt:.3f} — "
             f"{'at the theorem!' if abs(r_53-1/3)<0.02 else 'the maximum is hiding'}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Find the peak; it lands at $r = 1/3$, $C_P = 16/27$. Note what the
theorem forbids: $C_P = 1$ would require $r = 0$ — stopped air, which
cannot leave, so nothing new can arrive. **A perfect turbine is a wall.**
The wind's exit kinetic energy isn't waste; it's the *shipping cost* of
removing the spent air. This argument, three conservation laws and no
hardware, was settled in 1919 and every rotor since has been chasing its
ceiling.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"The force of the water" is not one thing. A bend's anchor carries
pressure forces *and* momentum-flux forces, and at typical plant
pressures the pressure part dominates — students who compute only $\dot m
\Delta V$ under-size anchors by multiples. Write every force on the CV
first; only then sum. The ledger has no line item called "the force of
the water."
:::

```{=html}
     data-solution="4 × 196 = 784 N. (Power went up 8×; storms are efficient vandals.)"

```

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Anchor force on the 90° bend?"
     data-answer="277" data-tol="0.03" data-units="N"
     data-hint="Momentum in and momentum out are perpendicular arrows of equal length ρAV². Draw them tip-to-tail: the change is the hypotenuse, √2 times ρAV²."
     data-solution="|ΔṁV| = √2 × ρAV² = 277 N at 45° between the legs. A 180° U-bend would pay 2× — full reversal is the expensive one."></div>
```

Stop, scale, turn: ρAV² with a vector diagram is nine-tenths of every anchor-bolt calculation you will ever sign.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** A firefighter's nozzle accelerates 30 L/s of water from 3 m/s to 25 m/s. What force does the crew brace against, momentum-flux only?</summary>
$\dot m \Delta V = 998 \times 0.03 \times 22 \approx 660$ N — about the
weight of a large adult, arriving as a steady shove. (The full answer
adds the gauge-pressure force at the nozzle inlet; try `nozzle_thrust`.)
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Why does the Betz analysis conclude the disk's local velocity is the *average* of $U_1$ and $U_2$ — what breaks if it weren't?</summary>
Equating the momentum result ($P = T \cdot U_\text{disk}$) with the
energy result ($P = \tfrac12 \dot m (U_1^2-U_2^2)$) forces $U_\text{disk}
= (U_1+U_2)/2$. Any other value makes the two conservation laws disagree
about the same power — not an option.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Two identical jets hit two plates: one plate held fixed, one retreating at half the jet speed. Compare the forces — and where did the "missing" momentum go?</summary>
The moving plate feels $(1/2)^2 = 1/4$ the force: relative velocity
enters *twice* (less mass intercepted per second, gentler turn). Nothing
is missing — the jet behind the retreating plate still carries momentum,
plus the plate is absorbing energy as *power* (this trade is Unit 10's
Pelton story, U = V/3 vs V/2 and all).
</details>

## Bring to class

The Betz peak sits at exactly $r = 1/3$. Come with the physical sentence —
no algebra — for why the optimum slows the wind by *two-thirds* rather
than stopping it, phrased so a rancher leasing land for turbines would nod.
